newsitem.title: GERMANY: German MP doubts court will back EMU complaint.
newsitem.headline: German MP doubts court will back EMU complaint.

text.p: The head of the German parliament's legal affairs committee said on Wednesday he doubted the supreme court would uphold a citizen's complaint filed this week against Europe's planned monetary union (EMU).

Horst Eylmann, a deputy from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), said the court was not the institution to decide whether other EU countries were using "creative accounting" that undermined the single currency.

A Munich journalist, Klaus Peter Heim, filed the complaint in advance with the Karlsruhe-based Federal Constitutional Court on Tuesday, the first of several challenges expected to be made in Germany once the first wave of EMU members is decided next year.

Heim said he wanted the court to review and reject EU decisions allowing what he called "accounting tricks" by France and Italy to help them meet the Maastricht treaty's strict budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
That would mean that EMU would not meet the criteria for lasting stability that the court and the Bonn parliament say are needed for Germany to join it, he said.
Asked on Saarland Radio what the complaint's chances were, Eylmann said: "I think its chances are small.

"These are political questions and, according to the constitution, parliament is the body that decides them. How can one seriously assume that eight judges in Karlsruhe can decide the issue better than parliament and the government?"

Heim's complaint does not mention Bonn's plans to sell off shares in Deutsche Telekom or revalue the Bundesbank's gold and currency reserves, two moves critics have said amounts to "creative accounting" on Germany's part.
Eylmann, who defended both steps, said he was not surprised by the complaint. "It would be a miracle if nobody brought a complaint against the euro."
